title: Benchmark Report Launch — Sales/SE Objection Handling Notes (working)
content:
Context
- Doc purpose: quick working notes for AEs/SEs on expected pushback during benchmark report conversations (esp. latency/$), with draft responses + what NOT to claim.
- Audience: Sales, SE, SDRs, CS (inbound). This is not customer-facing copy.
- Source inputs: Methodology doc + Claims Guidelines + Competitive FAQ (links above). Some phrasing here still needs Soojin/Legal final pass.

Core framing (use this upfront)
- “This report is about production economics: latency per dollar, with supporting latency/throughput/cost metrics. It’s designed to be reproducible and comparable across regions.”
- “We publish methodology + variance guidance because we expect real-world results to vary by workload, traffic shape, and region.”
- “If you want, we can help you run a smaller reproduction against your own prompts and target regions.”

Hard rules / red lines (do NOT say)
- Do not claim: “fastest” or “best” overall without qualifiers and without pointing to the published scope + confidence/variance language.
- Do not claim: results generalize to every workload. Always anchor: “for the workloads and settings defined in the methodology.”
- Do not imply competitor malfeasance or “their numbers are fake.” Keep it methodological.
- Do not share raw per-request logs, traces, or internal run IDs outside Redwood.

Top objections + draft responses

1) “Latency/$ is a weird metric — why not just cost per 1M tokens?”
What they mean
- Procurement wants simple cost. Engineers care about responsiveness. They suspect we’re hiding something.
Draft response
- “Cost-per-token is useful, but it can mask slow serving. Latency/$ intentionally forces the tradeoff into one view: how much latency you get for a given spend. We also publish the underlying p50/p95 latency and cost metrics so you can sanity-check.”
Follow-up question (qualify)
- “Are you bound by a user-visible p95 latency SLO, or by a monthly budget cap? Often teams have both.”
Proof points to reference
- Methodology section where we show derived metric and component metrics (p50/p95 + $/1M tokens).

2) “The numbers will change tomorrow — open models and infra move fast. Why should I trust a point-in-time report?”
Draft response
- “Agree that everything moves. That’s why we treat this as a benchmark with a defined harness, environment controls, and variance analysis — not a one-off screenshot. The report includes date range and rerun policy, and we plan a refresh cadence so you can track deltas.”
- “For purchase decisions, we can validate in a controlled trial in your target regions with your traffic shape.”
Qualifying
- “Are you evaluating for a near-term launch (next 30–60 days) or longer-term platform choice?”
Action
- Offer reproduction guidance + Dedicated/Private evaluation plan.

3) “Variance seems high / I don’t believe the confidence intervals.”
Draft response
- “We expect variance in multi-tenant and even dedicated environments due to GPU scheduling, network jitter, and batch formation. The report’s variance section exists so you can interpret differences that are within noise vs meaningful.”
- “If a delta is within the variance bands, we don’t call it a win. When variance exceeded thresholds, we reran and investigated (and we document rerun rules).”
SE deeper detail (only if asked)
- “We use repeated runs, exclude warmup, and compute summary stats across runs. We trigger reruns when run-to-run dispersion crosses the documented threshold.”
Landmine to avoid
- Don’t promise “zero variance.” Instead: “predictability via Dedicated capacity + SLO guardrails.”

4) “Your region results don’t match what I’m seeing.”
Likely causes
- They’re hitting a different region than they think.
- Their prompt/sequence length distribution differs materially.
- They’re using streaming vs non-streaming and comparing ‘time-to-first-token’ vs end-to-end.
- Concurrency profile is different (spiky vs steady).
Draft response
- “Totally possible. Region performance is sensitive to where requests enter, traffic shape, and the request mix. The report uses a specific region selection + concurrency distribution. Let’s confirm which region you’re actually routed to and compare the same metric (TTFT vs full completion).”
Checklist (SE)
- Confirm region header/config.
- Confirm model version.
- Confirm streaming on/off and metric definition.
- Confirm concurrency and output length settings.
- Confirm caching/batching behaviors (customer app vs our harness).
Offer
- “We can run a short controlled test in your target region(s) with your prompt distribution to reconcile.”

5) “This workload doesn’t look like mine (we do short prompts / long contexts / tool calls / RAG / JSON).”
Draft response
- “The report intentionally uses representative baseline workloads so results are comparable. If your workload differs (e.g., long context, structured output), the ranking can change. The report is a starting point, not the last word.”
- “We can tailor a reproduction run: same harness but with your context lengths and completion targets.”
Qualifying questions
- “What are your typical input tokens (p50/p95) and output tokens?”
- “Do you care more about TTFT, p95 end-to-end, or throughput at a given concurrency?”
- “Do you use function/tool calling and require strict JSON? What’s your failure tolerance?”

6) “You must have tuned specifically for your benchmark harness.”
Draft response
- “We’re explicit about the runtime settings used so others can reproduce. The goal is production realism: stable settings, not one-off tuning. When we change defaults for consistency, we document it.”
- “If you’re worried about overfitting, the best check is to run your own prompt set using the published recipe. We’ll help you do that.”
Proof
- Point to methodology + ‘how to reproduce’ guide (public) and internal runbook (do not share internal runbook externally).

7) “Competitor X says your comparison is unfair / they’d do better with different settings.”
Draft response
- “That may be true for some workloads. We can only compare under a defined, published test. The report describes those settings, and we avoid claims outside that scope.”
- “If you want an apples-to-apples evaluation for your workload, we can run a joint test plan: your prompts, your target regions, and clearly defined metrics.”
Don’t
- Don’t speculate about competitor internal configs.

8) “Are you hiding reliability issues? Benchmarks ignore error rates and tail behavior.”
Draft response
- “We agree reliability matters. During benchmark windows we monitor error rates and tail latency, and we publish p95 (and include notes on guardrails). For production, we typically recommend Dedicated if you need tighter tail + predictable throughput.”
Qualifying
- “Do you have an SLO for success rate/timeouts?”
- “Do you need canary/fallback policies?”
Tie-in
- Redwood Console rollouts + fallback routing, plus Dedicated SLAs.

9) “Pricing assumptions look cherry-picked (e.g., discounts, reserved capacity).”
Draft response
- “The report uses a documented pricing basis for comparability. We separate the measured performance from the cost model inputs, and we’re clear about what’s included/excluded.”
- “If you’re buying Dedicated or have committed spend, your effective $/token changes; we can model your scenario separately and still use the same latency measurements.”
Escalate
- If they push on contract specifics, loop in AE + Sales Ops / pricing.

10) “This doesn’t address data residency / security. Can we even use this?”
Draft response
- “The report doesn’t use or expose customer data. It’s run on benchmark prompts. For residency, we publish results per region and offer Dedicated/Private options depending on your requirements.”
- “We have a security/data handling FAQ we can share alongside the report.”
Qualifying
- “Do you require EU-only processing? VPC? On-prem? Specific audit/retention controls?”

11) “How do you compute latency — client-side, server-side? What about network?”
Draft response
- “We define measurement points in the methodology. In general, we separate server-side processing from client overhead where possible, and we use consistent clients per region to keep comparisons fair.”
SE detail (only if asked)
- “We report p50/p95 under defined concurrency and exclude warmup. Where network is included, it’s consistent across runs in that region.”
If they need more
- Offer a technical deep dive with Perf/Evals or SE.

12) “Your p95 looks good but our users complain about spikes.”
Draft response
- “p95 is a summary; bursts can still happen. We can look at your traffic shape and routing policy (region selection, fallback behavior) and recommend settings that reduce spikes: Dedicated capacity, autoscaling policies, and guardrails.”
Tactical next step
- Ask for a sample of timestamps + request metadata (non-sensitive) to correlate with region health.

Conversation flows (practical)

A) Inbound from report download (SDR/AEs)
- Start: “What model(s) and region(s) are you considering, and what’s the user-visible latency target?”
- If they say “just evaluating”: offer 15-min “economics consult” + reproduction plan.
- If they say “vendor bake-off”: propose a joint test plan based on their prompts.

B) Active deal (SE-led)
- Map their constraints: context length distribution, concurrency, p95 SLO, region/residency, reliability.
- Pick 1–2 relevant report charts (don’t overwhelm).
- Offer: short benchmark reproduction + “what would Dedicated look like” sizing.

Quick qualifier prompts (copy/paste)
- “What are your p50/p95 input tokens and output tokens?”
- “Which metric matters most: TTFT, end-to-end p95, or throughput at concurrency N?”
- “Which regions must you serve from (and do you need residency guarantees)?”
- “Do you expect steady traffic or bursty traffic?”
- “Is quality pinned to a specific model/version or can we propose variants/quant profiles?”

Internal TODOs / open questions (as of 2/19)
- Need approved sentence for: “variance bands / confidence” wording (Sana + Legal).
- Confirm which regions we are highlighting publicly as ‘APAC’ (Tokyo vs Singapore) so reps don’t overpromise.
- Add 2–3 example ‘good’ customer questions to the landing page FAQ (Wei/Elliot).
- Decide if we want a standard ‘test plan template’ one-pager for bake-offs.

Owner notes (Markus)
- Goal is to keep reps from arguing about individual datapoints. If a prospect wants to litigate methodology, pivot to: define their workload + run a controlled reproduction.
- If you hear repeated confusion on any of the above, drop notes in #sales-enablement and tag me + Soojin so we can update the official FAQ.
